title: Instagram System Architecture
description: A photo and video sharing social platform supporting billions of daily media uploads, personalized feed generation, and real-time engagement.
summary:
### 1. Media Upload & Processing Pipeline

Handles the ingestion and storage of user-uploaded photos and videos. The client requests a pre-signed URL from the Post Service and uploads the media directly to Object Storage (S3). The Post Service saves the metadata (caption, user_id, etc.) in a sharded relational database (PostgreSQL) and publishes a 'new post' event to Kafka to trigger asynchronous processes like feed generation and video transcoding. Video transcoding is handled by a dedicated async worker service that processes the raw video into multiple renditions.

### 2. Feed Generation & Read Path

Focuses on serving a user's personalized news feed with low latency (<200ms). A hybrid fan-out approach is used: for normal users with a moderate number of followers, posts are pre-computed and pushed to a **Feed Timeline** table (Cassandra) and cached in Redis (fan-out-on-write). For celebrity users with millions of followers, posts are fetched on-demand (fan-in-on-read) and merged with the cached feed for the user. The Feed Service retrieves post IDs from the timeline and then fetches the full post metadata, with results served from the Redis cache.

### 3. Engagement & Notification Service

Manages user interactions (likes, comments) and notifications. The Engagement Service asynchronously processes likes and comments via a message queue (Kafka) to update databases and caches. The Notification Service consumes events from Kafka and sends push notifications to users via APNs/FCM. The system uses a **sharded relational database** for core data (posts, users, comments) and a **wide-column store (Cassandra)** for feed timelines, optimized for fast sequential reads. Elasticsearch is used for full-text search and indexing of posts and user profiles, with results cached in Redis for performance.

functional: Users can upload photos and videos, which are stored durably with 11 9s of reliability using multipart upload for resumability
Users can follow/unfollow other users and view a personalized news feed of recent posts from followed accounts
Users can like, comment, and share posts, and receive push notifications for these interactions
Users can search for other users and posts based on captions or hashtags with full-text search
The system must support ephemeral stories that disappear after 24 hours with separate expiration logic
nonFunctional: High availability — the service must be available 99.99% of the time with no single point of failure and multi-region replication
Low latency — News Feed generation must complete within 200ms globally, with Redis absorbing the read path
Massive scalability — the system must handle hundreds of millions of daily active users and billions of read/write operations
Eventual consistency — it is acceptable for a slight delay in showing new posts or likes, in favor of availability and performance

stages.title: The MVP — direct upload, one database, one bucket
stages.narrative:
Every social platform starts simple. A stateless Post Service issues **pre-signed URLs** so clients upload photos directly into S3 — media bytes never touch the API tier. Metadata (caption, user_id, timestamp) lands in a sharded **PostgreSQL** instance.

Timelines are naive: the client requests recent posts from followed users and the database runs a join across the follow graph. This works for a few thousand users, but every feed read is an expensive multi-table query, and every viewer downloads the full-size original photo — a slow, wasteful experience.

stages.title: Feed pre-computation and video transcoding
stages.trigger: Views outnumber uploads 200:1 and every feed read joins across the entire follow graph — database queries take seconds for users with thousands of follows
stages.narrative:
Stop computing feeds at read time. The Post Service now publishes a **'new post' event** to Kafka. A Feed Worker consumes it and writes the post ID to every follower's timeline in **Cassandra** — partitioned by `user_id`, clustered by `created_at`, so reading the top N posts is a single sequential scan.

Video uploads get the same decoupling: a **Video Transcoder** consumes the same event and processes raw videos into multiple renditions asynchronously. The Feed Service (behind its own API Gateway) serves the pre-computed timeline, and the system now scales read traffic without crushing the relational database.

stages.title: Engagement, search, and notifications
stages.trigger: Likes and comments produce 115K writes/sec at peak — synchronous processing would stall the API servers
stages.narrative:
Social interactions are write-heavy and latency-tolerant, which makes them a natural fit for the same async pattern. The **Engagement Service** processes likes, comments, and shares by publishing events to a dedicated Kafka topic. Workers consume these events to update counters in Redis (fast reads) and materialize rows in PostgreSQL (durable storage).

A **Search Service** backed by **Elasticsearch** indexes post captions and user profiles for full-text search. The **Notification Service** consumes engagement events and delivers push notifications via APNs/FCM. Every new subsystem is decoupled by the same queue — the architecture's async backbone.

stages.title: Scale with caching and hybrid fan-out
stages.trigger: Celebrities with 100M followers cause a write explosion — fanning out a single post to every follower's timeline writes 100M rows
stages.narrative:
Two optimizations finish the architecture. First, a **Redis cache** in front of the feed timeline stores each user's top 100 post IDs in memory — the hottest reads never touch Cassandra. Second, a **hybrid fan-out** strategy switches celebrity accounts to fan-in-on-read: their posts are NOT pre-written to followers' timelines; instead, the Feed Service merges them from a dedicated **Posts DB** at read time.

With these additions, the system handles the full Instagram scale: 500M DAUs, 500M new posts per day, 10B likes, and sub-200ms feed generation for every user — whether they follow 200 people or 200 million.

decisions.title: Clients upload media directly
decisions.rationale: Video and image uploads can be gigabytes in size. If these bytes flowed through the API tier, it would have to scale with *media traffic* instead of *request traffic*, making it expensive and slow. Pre-signed URLs offload the bandwidth and latency cost to the object storage, while the API tier only handles small metadata requests. Multipart upload adds resumability for free: a failed chunk retries alone.

decisions.title: Feed generation strategy
decisions.choice: Hybrid fan-out (write for normal, read for celebrities)
alternatives: Fan-out on write for all users
Fan-in on read for all users
decisions.rationale: Fan-out on write for all users would cause massive write amplification for celebrities with millions of followers — 100M writes per post. Fan-in on read for all users would make feed reads too slow due to many joins per request. The hybrid approach balances this: most users get fast pre-computed feeds from Cassandra/Redis, while celebrity accounts use on-demand reads to avoid the 'write explosion' problem.

decisions.title: PhotoID generation
decisions.choice: Epoch time + auto-increment in a dedicated key generation service
decisions.rationale: To uniquely identify photos and avoid collisions across shards, we need a globally unique ID. Using epoch time as the most significant bits allows sorting photos by time naturally, and an auto-increment sequence ensures uniqueness. This also enables efficient retrieval of recent posts from a specific user through a sequential index scan.

decisions.title: Data sharding strategy
decisions.choice: Partition based on PhotoID for even distribution
decisions.rationale: Sharding by UserID keeps all photos of a user on one shard, but creates 'hot spots' for popular users. Sharding by PhotoID with a consistent hash ensures even data distribution and avoids any single shard being overwhelmed by a celebrity's uploads. It also simplifies adding new shards for future growth without rebalancing.

decisions.title: Async video processing and engagement
decisions.choice: Dedicated worker services consuming from Kafka queues
alternatives: Process engagement inline in the API
decisions.rationale: Video transcoding is CPU-intensive, and engagement writes peak at 115K/sec. Processing either synchronously would block the API server and degrade user experience. By decoupling through Kafka, uploads and engagement actions return instantly, the worker fleets scale independently on queue depth, and failed jobs retry without affecting the user-facing API.

decisions.title: Cassandra for feed timelines
decisions.rationale: The feed timeline workload is write-heavy (fan-out) and requires fast sequential reads of the top N posts — a natural fit for Cassandra's partitioned row storage. PostgreSQL would require complex sharding for the same throughput. Redis lacks the durability and capacity for all users' full timelines, so it works as a cache atop Cassandra, not a replacement.

bottlenecks.title: Feed: Celebrity post 'write explosion'
bottlenecks.problem: When a celebrity with 100 million followers posts a photo, fan-out-on-write would require 100 million writes to the followers' timelines. This could overwhelm Cassandra and Kafka queues simultaneously, causing backpressure across the entire async pipeline.
bottlenecks.mitigation: The hybrid fan-out approach switches celebrities to fan-in-on-read: their posts are fetched from the Posts DB at read time and merged with the cached feed. This avoids the write spike for popular accounts while keeping read latency under 200ms.

bottlenecks.title: Engagement: Thundering herd on viral posts
bottlenecks.problem: A viral post can receive millions of likes and comments within minutes. The engagement service, notification service, and databases all see a massive surge — enough to saturate connections and cause cascading timeouts.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Kafka decouples ingestion from processing. The Engagement Service writes each action to the queue almost instantly, then workers drain it asynchronously with batching. Redis caches running counts so reads never hit the database during the storm.

bottlenecks.title: Feed: Cassandra hot partitions
bottlenecks.problem: Partitioning the feed timeline by `user_id` spreads load for most users, but a celebrity with millions of followers still creates a single hot partition when their followers read simultaneously.
bottlenecks.mitigation: The Redis cache absorbs nearly all reads for hot keys. For celebrity fan-in, the read path goes to the Posts DB rather than the timeline at all — Cassandra only stores pre-computed timelines for normal users.

bottlenecks.title: Media: High cost of storage and egress
bottlenecks.problem: With 500M new posts per day, storing and serving petabytes of media becomes extremely expensive, especially serving content directly from blob storage to millions of viewers.
bottlenecks.mitigation: A multi-tiered storage strategy: hot tier (frequently accessed content) and cold tier (older content). A global CDN caches media closer to users, reducing egress costs and latency by 90-95% for cache hits. Direct S3 URLs serve as the fallback for rarely-viewed content.

quiz.question: Why are pre-signed URLs used for media uploads, instead of uploading through the application servers?
quiz.answer: Pre-signed URLs allow the client to upload directly to blob storage (S3). This saves the application servers from processing heavy media traffic (gigabytes per upload), which would require the API tier to scale with bandwidth rather than request count. Pre-signed URLs keep the API tier small, stateless, and cheap.

quiz.question: What problem does the hybrid fan-out approach solve in Instagram's feed generation?
quiz.answer: It balances the trade-off between fast reads and heavy writes. For normal users, fan-out-on-write pre-computes the feed for lightning-fast reads. For celebrities with millions of followers, fan-in-on-read avoids the massive write amplification (100M writes per post). This hybrid strategy ensures both low latency for most users and system stability.

quiz.question: Why is a sharded relational database (PostgreSQL) used for user and post metadata rather than a document database?
quiz.answer: User, post, and comment data is highly relational (users follow users, posts are owned by users, comments belong to posts). A relational database with ACID transactions ensures consistency for these core relationships — critical for follows and post creation. Cassandra handles the feed timeline instead because that workload is write-heavy and key-partitioned, needing no joins.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of using a wide-column store like Cassandra for the feed timeline?
quiz.answer: Cassandra is optimized for high-volume writes and fast sequential reads. The feed timeline table is partitioned by user_id and clustered by created_at, making it efficient to write a new post ID to every follower's timeline and later read the top N posts in a single sequential scan. Its distributed design also ensures high availability and write throughput.

quiz.question: Why is Redis used as a cache atop Cassandra rather than as the primary feed store?
quiz.answer: Cassandra provides persistent, durable storage for every user's full timeline at Instagram's scale. Redis, being an in-memory cache, cannot economically store all users' complete timelines. Instead, Redis caches the top ~100 feed posts per user, providing millisecond reads for the hottest data while Cassandra backs the long tail.

quiz.question: What happens to the read path when the Redis feed cache misses?
quiz.answer: On a cache miss, the Feed Service reads from Cassandra directly, back-fills the result into Redis for the next request, and returns the feed. The first read after a cache expiration is slightly slower (~10-12ms vs ~1ms), but subsequent reads are fast again. The system degrades gracefully — latency increases, but nothing breaks.

quiz.question: Why is Kafka used for both feed fan-out and engagement processing?
quiz.answer: Both workloads share the same shape: a burst of writes that must be durably recorded and processed asynchronously. Kafka buffers these bursts (a celebrity post or a viral like storm), decouples producers from consumers, gives failed jobs a retry path, and lets each worker fleet autoscale independently on queue depth.

nodes.name: Client (Mobile/Web)
nodes.details:
The client is responsible for media capture and upload orchestration.

- Compresses and splits media into chunks before uploading
- Requests **pre-signed URLs** from the Post Service before uploading
- Uploads each chunk directly to S3; a failed chunk retries independently
- Views the personalized feed by calling the Feed Service via the API Gateway

nodes.name: API Gateway
nodes.details:
Single entry point for the upload control plane.

- Authenticates every request before routing to the Post Service
- Enforces per-client rate limits to protect backend services
- Terminates TLS at the gateway boundary
- Routes to stateless Post Service instances

nodes.name: Post Service
nodes.details:
Stateless service that owns the upload control plane.

- Authenticates the user and initiates a multipart upload session in S3
- Generates **pre-signed URLs** so the client can upload directly to S3
- Writes post metadata (caption, user_id, S3 path) to the sharded PostgreSQL
- Publishes a `post.created` event to Kafka for downstream consumers
- Never touches the actual media bytes — the data path goes directly from client to S3

failure.userImpact: No new posts can be created — the control plane for uploads is down. Existing posts and feed reads continue working because the read path is independent.

blastRadius.note: health checks fail; no healthy instances to route to
no events published; feed workers and transcoder idle

failure.mitigation: The Post Service is **stateless** — autoscaling replaces failed instances within seconds. The gateway's health checks eject unhealthy instances, so the realistic failure is a brief brownout, not a blackout. No data is lost because Kafka producers buffer events locally during an outage.

nodes.name: Object Storage (S3)
nodes.details:
Durable, highly available blob storage for all uploaded media.

- Receives media chunks **directly from clients** via pre-signed URLs
- Assembles the final object when the multipart upload completes
- Emits `s3:ObjectCreated` events that the async pipeline consumes
- Stores originals permanently; transcoded variants live in a separate bucket

nodes.name: Metadata DB (PostgreSQL)
nodes.details:
Sharded relational database for core application data.

- Stores users, posts, comments, follows, and likes as relational data
- Partitioned by **PhotoID** (or UserID for user data) to distribute load
- ACID transactions guarantee consistency for follows and post creation
- Each shard is a primary-replica pair for high availability
- Not used for feed timelines — that workload belongs to Cassandra

failure.userImpact: Core functionality breaks: no new posts, no likes, no comments, no follows. Existing feed data cached in Cassandra and Redis remains readable but cannot be updated.

blastRadius.note: cannot save metadata; uploads stall at the metadata step
celebrity fan-in reads fail without access to post data

failure.mitigation: Each shard runs a **primary-replica** pair with automated failover. A single shard loss takes down only that partition's data, not the entire system. The read path (feeds served from Cassandra/Redis) continues serving cached content — the outage is limited to writes and metadata reads for the affected shard.

nodes.name: Message Queue (Kafka)
nodes.details:
The async backbone of the upload pipeline.

- Receives `post.created` events from the Post Service
- Decouples the upload path from feed fan-out, video transcoding, and search indexing
- Provides at-least-once delivery guarantees with ordered partitions per user
- Queue depth is the autoscaling signal for downstream consumers

failure.userImpact: Uploads complete and metadata persists, but videos are never transcoded, feeds never update, and search indexes stall. Creators see confirmation but followers never see the new post.

blastRadius.note: no events to consume — video processing halts
no events to consume — feed timeline stops updating

failure.mitigation: Managed Kafka (Confluent/MSK) provides multi-node replication with automatic leader failover. Producers buffer events locally during a broker outage. The honest backstop is a **reconciliation job** that periodically scans S3 for objects with no matching processed post and re-enqueues them, ensuring nothing is permanently lost.

nodes.name: Video Transcoder
nodes.details:
Consumes `post.created` events and processes video uploads into streamable formats.

- Polls Kafka for new video upload events
- Downloads the raw video from S3, transcodes it into multiple resolutions
- Uploads processed renditions back to a transcoded output bucket
- Scales horizontally on queue depth

nodes.name: Client (Mobile/Web)
nodes.details:
The feed-facing client.

- Requests the user's home feed via the Feed Service
- Displays a paginated, infinitely scrolling list of posts ordered by time
- Pull-to-refresh triggers a new feed request with the latest cursor
- Renders cached posts immediately while the network request resolves

nodes.name: API Gateway
nodes.details:
Entry point for feed read traffic.

- Authenticates the user and routes to the Feed Service
- Rate-limits aggressive polling (one request per 30s minimum interval)
- Terminates TLS for feed requests

nodes.name: Feed Service
nodes.details:
The core read-path service — implements the hybrid fan-out strategy.

- For normal users: reads pre-computed post IDs from Redis cache (>cache hit) or Cassandra timeline (cache miss)
- For celebrity follows: queries the Posts DB directly (fan-in-on-read) and merges results into the timeline
- Assembles full post metadata (caption, media URL, like count) by fetching from the appropriate source
- Returns paginated results with a cursor; total generation must complete in under 200ms
- Every cache miss triggers a **back-fill** to Redis for the next request

failure.userImpact: Every feed request fails — the app shows stale cached content or an empty state. Users cannot discover new posts from followed accounts.

blastRadius.note: health checks fail; no healthy instances to route feed requests to
unused while Feed Service is down — cache entries expire without refill

failure.mitigation: The Feed Service is **stateless** and scales behind the gateway. Autoscaling replaces failed instances quickly. The cached data in Redis survives a full service restart — when the service comes back, cache hits return immediately while back-fill logic re-warms cold entries.

nodes.name: Feed Timeline (Cassandra)
nodes.details:
Wide-column store for pre-computed feed timelines.

- Partitioned by `user_id`, clustered by `created_at` descending
- Each row is a single post ID — lightweight and write-optimized
- The Feed Worker writes a new row to every follower's partition on each new post
- Reading the top 100 posts is a single sequential scan within one partition — very fast
- Provides linear horizontal scalability for the write-heavy fan-out workload

failure.userImpact: Feeds cannot be read from the primary timeline store. Users see either a degraded empty feed or whatever remains in the Redis cache before entries expire.

blastRadius.note: cache entries expire without a primary store to refill from
feed generation falls back to celebrity-only fan-in or fails

failure.mitigation: Cassandra replicates data across multiple nodes and racks. A single-node loss is transparent — replicas serve reads and writes continue. The Redis cache buys time by serving hot feed entries even while the cluster heals. The hybrid fan-out also means celebrity account followers still get content via the Posts DB read path.

nodes.name: Feed Cache (Redis)
nodes.details:
In-memory cache that absorbs the hottest feed reads.

- Stores each user's top ~100 feed post IDs in a sorted set (ZSET)
- Cache hit → post IDs returned in ~1ms, Cassandra never touched
- Cache miss → read from Cassandra, back-fill Redis for the next request
- Not the source of truth — data loss means cold reads from Cassandra, not data loss
- TTL-based expiration ensures stale entries eventually refresh

failure.userImpact: Nothing breaks for most users — but every feed read now lands on Cassandra, increasing p99 latency from 1ms to ~12ms. Redis is a cache, not a source of truth.

blastRadius.note: absorbs 100% of feed reads instead of ~5% — hot partitions saturate first
response time climbs as every request waits on Cassandra

failure.mitigation: Redis is a **read-through cache**, not the source of truth. Losing it costs latency, not data. Cassandra keeps serving, replicas blunt the increased load, and the cache re-warms itself key by key as reads back-fill it. A Redis replica can be promoted quickly in a managed deployment.

nodes.name: Posts DB (PostgreSQL)
nodes.details:
Serves the fan-in-on-read path for celebrity accounts.

- The same sharded PostgreSQL that stores all post metadata
- For celebrity accounts, the Feed Service queries this directly instead of reading from Cassandra
- Returns only the most recent N posts from the celebrity — lightweight and fast
- Avoids the write explosion of fanning out one post to millions of timeline entries

nodes.name: Feed Worker
nodes.details:
The fan-out-on-write engine.

- Consumes `post.created` events from Kafka
- For each new post, looks up the creator's follower list
- Writes the post ID to every follower's timeline partition in Cassandra
- Writes the post ID to the Redis cache for the creator's own feed
- For celebrities, **skips** the fan-out (the read path handles it via fan-in)

nodes.name: Client (Mobile/Web)
nodes.details:
Handles social interactions and search.

- Sends like/comment/share actions to the Engagement Service
- Displays engagement counts (likes, comment count) cached in Redis
- Sends search queries to the Search Service
- Receives push notifications from APNs/FCM

nodes.name: API Gateway
nodes.details:
Entry point for engagement and search traffic.

- Routes engagement actions to the Engagement Service
- Routes search queries to the Search Service
- Enforces rate limits on likes (preventing spam) and search queries

nodes.name: Engagement Service
nodes.details:
Processes social interactions asynchronously.

- Receives like/comment/share actions from the client
- Publishes engagement events to Kafka for async processing
- Returns immediately to the client — the event is durably queued
- Updates in-memory counters in Redis for fast reads
- Never blocks the client on database writes

nodes.name: Message Queue (Kafka)
nodes.details:
The async backbone for engagement processing.

- Buffers engagement events during traffic spikes (up to 115K writes/sec)
- Decouples the Engagement Service from Engagement Workers and Notification Service
- Provides at-least-once delivery for engagement events
- Queue depth drives autoscaling for the worker fleet

failure.userImpact: Likes, comments, and shares appear to succeed (the client gets a 200) but never materialize — counters don't increment, notifications don't send. The system accepts writes but processing halts.

blastRadius.note: no events to consume — engagement counts stop updating
no events to consume — push notifications stop
stale counts served — never updated by worker

failure.mitigation: Managed Kafka provides multi-node replication with automatic failover. Engagement events persist on disk within Kafka — once the cluster recovers, the backlog drains and counters catch up. The client already shows optimistic counts, so the user-facing impact is limited to stale numbers.

nodes.name: Engagement Worker
nodes.details:
Consumes engagement events and materializes them.

- Reads engagement events from Kafka
- Batches writes to PostgreSQL for durable storage of likes and comments
- Updates Redis counters (like count, comment count) for the post
- Triggers notification events for the Notification Service

nodes.name: Engagement Cache (Redis)
nodes.details:
In-memory cache for engagement aggregates.

- Stores like counts, comment counts, and top comments per post
- Updated asynchronously by the Engagement Worker
- Provides millisecond reads for engagement metrics displayed alongside every post
- Reduces read load on PostgreSQL for the hottest engagement data

nodes.name: Search Service
nodes.details:
Full-text search service for users and posts.

- Accepts search queries (user search, caption/hashtag search) from the API Gateway
- Queries Elasticsearch for full-text matches
- Caches recent popular search results in Redis for fast repeat queries
- Returns ranked results matching the user's query

nodes.name: Search Index (Elasticsearch)
nodes.details:
Distributed search index for users and posts.

- Indexes post captions, hashtags, and user profiles for full-text search
- Supports typo-tolerant prefix and fuzzy matching
- Sharded across multiple nodes for performance and scale
- Updated asynchronously via events from Kafka

failure.userImpact: Search returns empty results or errors. Users cannot find posts by caption, hashtag, or search for other users by name.

blastRadius.note: no backing index to query — search becomes unavailable

failure.mitigation: Elasticsearch runs as a multi-node cluster with replica shards. A single node loss is transparent. The search cache in Redis keeps recent popular queries warm, so a brief outage only affects long-tail or first-time searches. When the cluster recovers, reindexing happens from the durable data stores.

nodes.name: Search Cache (Redis)
nodes.details:
Caches recent and popular search results.

- Stores results for recent user searches with a TTL
- Reduces load on Elasticsearch for repeated queries (autocomplete, trending hashtags)
- Clears stale entries to maintain result freshness

nodes.name: Notification Service
nodes.details:
Dispatches push notifications to users.

- Consumes notification events from Kafka (new like, new comment, new follower)
- Renders the notification message (e.g., 'UserX liked your photo')
- Sends via APNs (iOS) and FCM (Android)
- Handles batching to avoid rate limits from push notification providers
